rv.q: It's a worthy tribute to the music it loves – here's hoping the show can share it more widely.
Sporadically transcendent, mostly absurd, this folk musical sees a modern lesbian in New York find her true self by communing with her ballad-singing, proto-feminist female ancestors.
Ballad Lines must be one of the most exciting new musicals to hit the stage in some time.
These three connected stories are largely told through a tremendous score packed with new and traditional songs.
Ballad Lines is a strong folk musical that delivers stirring melodies and strong emotional connections.
The pacing is well judged, supported by a simple but effective set design that lets the performances and music remain central.
Ballad Lines has been nearly ten years in the making and shows a solidity and confidence in itself that is wonderful to witness.

You warm to the impetus behind a musical about the prevalence of ballads over time as a communal lifeline while at the same time hoping for further rewrites that would let a sometimes clotted evening flow as freely as its adventuresome score.

Ballad Lines is powerful and strong and doesn’t shy away from tough topics which are still relevant in todays society. It takes audiences on an emotional journey. The powerful storytelling is woven through the script and lyrics with the show being mostly sung through.
This has all the ingredients to make the next great musical.
Ballad Lines boasts one of the most impressive scores from any new musical in a number of years, and is undoubtedly the strongest element of a show that is pretty much in good shape throughout.

Overall, Ballad Lines is a celebratory night out with a great deal of heart, a beautifully realised musical with an immensely talented cast and musicians, and a score that lingers long after the final note.

The problem is that we can’t really invest in Sarah, or anyone else for that matter. In her very first scene, she is sentimental about keeping hold of a pink neon ‘good vibes’ sign and a giant cuddly panda, yet that doesn’t extend to her Aunt Betty’s box.
There is undeniably rich material here, but Finn Anderson and Tania Azevedo need to do as their protagonist does and look at the piece's component parts and decide what story they want to tell.

cn.t: Critics praise the impressive score and technical achievement, but note an empathy gap and clotted storytelling that prevent full emotional connection. A worthy tribute with strong music that needs tighter focus.
